title: Family Cyber Defense
intro: Every knight needs a strong castle. Let's lock down the basics that protect your whole family.

questions.prompt: I'll just give my best friend my password—

choices.text: That's fine, best friends can be trusted
choices.coach: Knight Rule number two! Passwords are secrets — even from your best friend.

choices.text: Keep it secret, even from your best friend
choices.coach: Friends change, passwords leak. Secret means secret.

choices.text: Share it but change it after a week
choices.coach: Once shared, you can't take it back — best to never share it at all.

questions.prompt: Pixel! It's me, Shieldy! Send me your password, quick!

choices.text: Send it, Shieldy needs it urgently
choices.coach: Real Shieldy would NEVER ask for a password. Urgency + password request = scam.

choices.text: Refuse — no one legitimate ever needs your password
choices.coach: Locked! Not even real friends or trusted adults ever need your actual password.

choices.text: Send half of it to be safe
choices.coach: There's no 'safe partial' sharing — just don't send it at all.

questions.prompt: What's a family code word for, exactly?

choices.coach: It's a real safety tool, not just a game — used to verify identity in emergencies.

choices.text: Verifying someone's identity in an unexpected or urgent call/message
choices.coach: Exactly right — especially important now that voices can be AI-cloned.
It should be refreshed and reused whenever verification is needed — not a one-time thing.

questions.prompt: Something online felt weird, but I don't want to get in trouble for telling my parent.

choices.coach: You are never in trouble for telling a trusted adult something felt wrong.

choices.text: Screenshot it and tell them anyway
choices.coach: Exactly the Knight move. Reporting is never punished in a Knight household.

choices.text: Only tell if it happens again
choices.coach: Tell the first time — don't wait for a pattern.

questions.prompt: Should your online accounts use the same password as each other?

choices.text: Yes, one password is easier to remember
choices.coach: If one account is ever breached, a reused password puts every other account at risk too.

choices.text: No — different passwords for different accounts
choices.coach: Exactly right — this limits the damage if one account is ever compromised.

choices.text: Only reuse it for unimportant accounts
choices.coach: There's no truly 'unimportant' account when it comes to password reuse.

questions.prompt: Final Knight Rule: what's the golden rule of Family Cyber Defense?

choices.coach: The goal is safe use, not avoidance — the internet can be great with the right habits.

choices.text: Passwords are secret, code words verify identity, and telling a grown-up is always safe
choices.coach: Shield up! That's the whole castle wall, right there.

choices.text: Only trust people you've met in person once
choices.coach: Even people you've met can be impersonated — verification habits matter more than a single meeting.
